name: tarp lean-to shelter: sloped tarp roof seen from above held by poles, open front with dark inside, bedroll and crate
label: wasteland_ruins/lean-to

surfaces.part: tarp roof (sloped plane with highlight and shading bands)
bedroll and crate inside the open front

answer.evidence: Rows 2-20 form a large sloped tarp roof seen from above. It has light top highlight bands (rows 2-8), a teal mid-slope and a blue patch, and it ends in a dark front-edge line at row 20. Row 21 is a very dark eave shadow (L=17), followed by the dark interior. Below the roof, rows 21-31 show the open south face: dark interior, wooden poles on both sides, and the bedroll and crate on the ground. That is about 10 rows of front face, so the roof reads as a top surface over a front opening, not a flat front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is much smaller than the references, so the call rests mostly on the measured facts. It has 17 visible tones per 16x16 tile against 12 and 10 for the references. Near-flat coverage is 0%, same as both references. Dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the outlines carry a tint, not a black sticker line. By eye, the tarp is mottled in several teal steps with lighter fold highlights and darker creases. The dark open front, the wooden poles, the crate and the bedroll are separated mostly by value and by dark tones of the neighbouring material. It has fewer steps and less grain than the tile roofs and stone wall, but it is not thinner or flatter than the references. I see no large flat fills and no uniform black outline.

The measured facts support this. It has 17 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10 for the references, and 0% near-flat coverage, the same as the references. 0% of its dark edge pixels are neutral, so the outlines lean toward the neighbouring material (dark teal beside the tarp, dark brown beside the wood) rather than being a black sticker line.
